summary: Defines application/multipart-core, a media type that combines representations of zero or more media types, each identified by a CoAP Content-Format, into one representation with little framing overhead.

eli5.summary: This is a small box with labeled compartments, so a tiny device can send several different things together in one package.

questions: how are multiple representations combined in coap
subtitle: A tiny binary container that lets one CoAP message carry several differently typed pieces of content.

tldr.problem: CoAP messages carry one representation with one Content-Format, but some applications need to combine several representations of different media types in a single message body.
tldr.mechanism: The application/multipart-core media type encodes the combination as a CBOR array of pairs: a Content-Format ID followed by a byte string holding that representation, or null if an optional part is absent.
tldr.outcome: Applications get a simple, efficient binary framing for multi-part bodies. IANA registered the media type and assigned it Content-Format ID 62.

facts.label: Array structure
facts.value: Even number of elements: ID, then byte string or null

today: RFC 8710 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2020. It is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC listed in the metadata, so it remains the definition of application/multipart-core.

sections.title: The Idea Behind Multipart Content-Format
sections.content:
RFC 8710 defines application/multipart-core, an application-independent media type that combines representations of zero or more different media types, each with a CoAP Content-Format identifier, into a single representation with minimal framing overhead. The name echoes the multipart media types of the original MIME specifications (RFC 2046), and its basic intent is like multipart/mixed. The semantics are relaxed so that collections can be ordered or unordered.

The RFC notes that recipients of multipart/mixed in email process parts in the listed order if they care about order, and ignore it otherwise, while multipart/parallel, meant for unordered collections, did not deploy.
sections.eli5: Email already had a way to stick several things in one message. This is a lighter version for small devices that speak CoAP.

sections.title: Three Ways to Use It
sections.content:
The detailed meaning of the parts comes from the context the application sets up, such as the resource URI and other options. Three usage scenarios are envisioned.

  • A sequence: the parts occur in order, for example audio snippets to be played in that order, or search results in order of relevance.
  • A bag: the parts are distinguished by their Content-Format identifiers, such as an audio snippet and an accompanying text representation, and order may not matter. A null value can stand in for an optional part that is not present.
  • A single choice: only one representation is present, with the sender picking one of several possible formats. The representation may also be optional, and omitting it gives a zero-length array.

When these rules are not enough, an application can reuse the format but register its own media type and Content-Format identifier for the more specific semantics. The RFC also notes that future specifications might define equivalents of other multipart types, such as multipart/alternative.
sections.eli5: You can send a list of things in order, a bag of things where order does not matter, or just one thing chosen from several possible kinds.

sections.title: The CBOR Encoding
sections.content:
A representation of this type holds a collection of zero or more representations, each with its Content-Format. The collection is a CBOR (RFC 7049) array with an even number of elements. Counting from zero, each even-numbered element is an unsigned integer giving a Content-Format ID. The odd-numbered element after it is a byte string holding the representation, or null if an optional part is indicated as not given.

The RFC's example is a collection with one representation of Content-Format ID 42 and one of Content-Format ID 0, written in CBOR diagnostic notation as [42, h'0123456789abcdef', 0, h'3031323334']. A CDDL description is given as multipart-core = [* multipart-part] with multipart-part = (type: uint .size 2, part: bytes / null).

The format is a strict specification. An implementation MUST stop processing if there is a CBOR well-formedness error, a deviation from the structure above, or any residual data left after processing the CBOR data item.
sections.eli5: The package is a list that goes: label, contents, label, contents. If the list is built wrong or has leftovers, the receiver must stop and not use it.

sections.title: Example: Observing Resources
sections.content:
The RFC shows a less obvious use, combined with observing a resource (RFC 7641) to handle pending results. If a client registers to observe a resource that has no representation yet, the server may send one or more 2.05 (Content) notifications indicating the lack of a representation. Later, the first actual 2.05 (Content) or 2.03 (Valid) notification is sent, and the sequence can end in a 4.xx or 5.xx response.

The Observe option requires that all notifications carry the same Content-Format. The multipart type can supply that Content-Format: an empty list of representations in the 'Pending' case, and a single representation of the target Content-Format once one is available.
sections.eli5: If you ask a friend to tell you when the cake is ready, they can keep sending an empty box while it bakes, and a box with cake in it when it is done. Every box looks the same from outside.

sections.title: Serialization Hints
sections.content:
This section is for readers new to CBOR and contains no new information. An empty collection is an empty CBOR array, serialized as the single byte 0x80. A collection with one representation is a two-element array, serialized as 0x82 followed by the Content-Format value and then the object as a byte string with its length in front.

For example, a single text/plain object (Content-Format 0) with the 11 characters 'Hello World' is serialized as 0x82 0x00 0x4b followed by the characters. For more representations the array head changes: 0x84 for two, 0x86 for three, and so on. The earlier example becomes 0x84 0x182A 0x48 0x0123456789ABCDEF 0x00 0x45 0x3031323334, where Content-Format 42 has byte string length 8 and Content-Format 0 has length 5.
sections.eli5: This section just shows how the labels and contents look as actual bytes: first a count of items, then each label, then how long the contents are, then the contents.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of CBOR (RFC 7049) apply. The RFC points out that resource exhaustion attacks may use large values in the byte string size fields, or deeply nested structures of recursively embedded application/multipart-core representations.
sections.eli5: Someone could send a box that claims to be huge, or boxes nested inside boxes inside boxes, to wear out a small device. Receivers should be careful.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the media type application/multipart-core (binary encoding, intended usage COMMON, change controller IESG), using the procedures of RFC 6838. The RFC names EST over secure CoAP as an example of an application that needs to combine representations. Fragment identifiers follow the rules for application/cbor.

IANA also registered Content-Format ID 62 for this type in the 'CoAP Content-Formats' subregistry of the 'Constrained RESTful Environments (CoRE) Parameters' registry.
sections.eli5: The official lists now include this package type and give it the number 62.
